summary: Friedrich Gottlieb Welcker worked in linguistics and history and archaeology. He studied at the University of Giessen (1801–1803) and held posts at Giessen (~1809–1816), Göttingen (~1816–1819), and Bonn (~1819–1859).

Friedrich Haag worked in Indology and linguistics. He studied at Zurich under Heinrich Schweizer-Sidler, Berlin, and Göttingen. He served at the Cathedral School of Tallinn, Kantonsschule Schaffhausen, Gymnasium Burgdorf, and the universities of Zurich and Bern.

Friedrich Heiler was a religious studies scholar who studied at the University of Munich (~1912–1917). He taught at the University of Munich (1918) and University of Marburg (1920), and directed the Religionskundliche Sammlung (~1927–1962).

Friedrich Hirth worked in Sinology and history and archaeology. He studied at Leipzig, Berlin, and Greifswald, and served in the Chinese Maritime Customs Service (1870–1897) before becoming Dean Lung Professor of Chinese at Columbia University (1902).
Friedrich Kurschat was a linguist who studied at the University of Königsberg from approximately 1834 to 1844 and held a post there from roughly 1841 to 1883.
Friedrich Leo worked in linguistics. He studied at Göttingen and Bonn under Hermann Usener. He held academic posts at Bonn, Kiel, Rostock, Strasbourg, and Göttingen (1889–1914).

Friedrich Majer worked in Indology and history and archaeology. He studied at the University of Jena (~1789–1792) and under Johann Gottfried von Herder, and later served as a Privatdozent at the University of Jena (~1799–1801).

Friedrich Max Müller was an Indologist, linguist, and religious studies scholar. He studied under Hermann Brockhaus, Eugène Burnouf, and Franz Bopp, among others. He was a Fellow of All Souls College and held professorships at Oxford (1850–1900).

Friedrich Müller worked in linguistics, Indology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Vienna under Anton Boller, Göttingen, and Tübingen, and held posts at the Austrian National Library and the University of Vienna (1858–1866, 1869).

Friedrich Nietzsche worked in philosophy and linguistics. He studied at Bonn and Leipzig, studying under Friedrich Wilhelm Ritschl, and held a faculty post at the University of Basel from 1869 to 1878.

Friedrich Otto Schrader worked in Indology and religious studies. He studied at the University of Strasbourg (~1898–1902), led the Adyar Library and Research Centre (1905–1916), and was professor of Indology at Kiel University (1921).
Friedrich Ottomar Eduard Wilhelm held academic posts at the University of Munich (~1910–1920) and the University of Freiburg (~1920–1922).

Friedrich Rückert worked in Indology, linguistics, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Würzburg, Heidelberg, and under Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall and Franz Bopp. He held posts at Jena, Erlangen-Nuremberg, and Berlin.

Friedrich Schleiermacher was a philosopher and religious studies scholar who studied at Halle-Wittenberg (~1787–1789). He later held posts at Halle-Wittenberg (~1804–1807) and the University of Berlin (~1810–1834).

Friedrich Schrader worked in Indology and history and archaeology. He completed his doctoral studies at the Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg under the supervision of Richard Pischel from approximately 1885 to 1889.

Friedrich Weller specialized in Indology, Buddhist studies, and Sinology. He studied at the University of Leipzig under August Conrady, later serving there as Privatdozent (~1922–1928) and chair of Indian Philology (1938–1958).

Friedrich Wilhelm worked in Indology and Tibetology, studying under Paul Thieme at the University of Munich. He held posts at the Bavarian Academy of Sciences and Munich (1963, 1969–1998), with guest professorships at Columbia and Collège de France.
Friedrich Wilhelm Graf is a religious studies scholar who held posts at the University of Augsburg (~1986–1999) and the University of Munich (~1999–2014).

Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling was a philosopher who studied at Tübingen and Leipzig. He held professorships at Jena, Würzburg, Erlangen-Nuremberg, Munich, and Berlin, and served as president of the Bavarian Academy of Sciences and Humanities.
Friedrich Wilhelm Karl Müller worked in Sinology, Buddhist studies, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied under Georg von der Gabelentz (~1889–1893) and Karl Foy.
